title: Multimodal VAEs for diabetes representation learning
summary: Two variational autoencoders trained on 380,000 patient-days of continuous glucose data, testing whether adding insulin and wearable signals produces a better representation than glucose alone.
context: Coursework project for a Probabilistic & Generative ML course (MSc), data from MetaboNet, a public harmonised dataset consolidating 21 Type 1 diabetes clinical studies

sections.heading: The problem
body: Diabetes care is assessed in snapshots (HbA1c every few months); metabolic state changes hour by hour.
list: Test whether unsupervised representation learning can organise patient-days by metabolic similarity, with zero clinical labels
Test whether adding insulin and wearable physiology to glucose alone produces a richer representation

sections.heading: Approach
body: Baseline: a CGM-only convolutional VAE. Multimodal version: fuses glucose, insulin, and wearable physiology through a Product-of-Experts layer, which combines each modality's posterior into one shared latent and handles missing modalities for free — important since wearable data only existed for a small slice of patients.
list: Data: 379,849 patient-days (13 studies) for training, 69,894 held-out days (305 patients) for evaluation
Main challenge — posterior collapse — addressed with a 32-dim latent space, KL annealing, and per-dimension free bits

images.alt: Product-of-Experts architecture: three encoders fusing into one shared latent distribution, then three decoders
images.caption: Product-of-Experts architecture — three encoders fuse into one shared latent, then three decoders reconstruct each modality.

sections.heading: Result
list: Both models converge on the same clinically interpretable latent axis — correlates with time-in-range, inversely with mean glucose — despite never seeing a clinical label
Multimodal did not clearly beat the baseline: worse patient-centroid alignment with glucose metrics (+0.448 vs +0.593 on time-in-range)
Cause: every evaluation metric was derived from CGM, biasing comparisons toward the CGM-only model
Insulin reconstruction also failed on sharp bolus events — MSE rewards predicting the average, not a spike

sections.heading: What the loss curves didn't show
body: A few early models looked healthy on train/validation loss while being completely broken underneath — only caught by digging into reconstructed traces, per-dimension KL values, and latent structure.
list: One decoder was only reconstructing the first few hours of each day
One checkpoint got selected before the KL term even kicked in — good reconstruction loss, totally unregularised latent space
The insulin encoder was partly responding to a normalisation artefact
